turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell raised a perfectly sculpted eyebrow, her gaze fixed upon Mr. Worthing with an air of profound skepticism. She inquired as to the precise location of this Belgrave Square residence, specifically requesting the street number, as if verifying its existence were a matter of the utmost urgency. It seemed, she intimated with a subtle tightening of her lips, that a gentleman’s veracity was to be tested with meticulous detail.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, feeling a slight warmth creep up his neck, responded that it was directly opposite the Albert Hall, a most respectable and convenient location, he assured Lady Bracknell.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing with a look of almost glacial disapproval. She inquired, with the air of one administering a most unpleasant but necessary duty, as to the precise nature of the Albert Hall’s connection to this residence, and whether its proximity might, perchance, suggest a regrettable lack of social refinement.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, feeling increasingly uncomfortable under Lady Bracknell’s gaze, hastened to assure her that the Albert Hall, while a magnificent edifice, simply provided a convenient landmark; the residence itself maintained a perfectly respectable distance, ensuring no undue influence from its grandeur, he explained.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell fixed Mr. Worthing with a stare that could curdle milk and inquired, with a delicate sniff, as to whether the Albert Hall, in its undeniable prominence, might not, in fact, attract a rather undesirable element. One must, she felt compelled to point out, be exceedingly careful to avoid association with anything remotely bohemian.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, attempting to regain some composure, hastened to explain that, naturally, the residents of Belgrave Square were a discerning and refined lot, entirely averse to anything remotely… bohemian. He assured Lady Bracknell that the proximity to the Albert Hall was, in fact, a testament to the area’s desirability, as it indicated a central, convenient location for those of quality. He hoped, with a slight tremor in his voice, that this clarified the matter.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing’s explanation with a skepticism that bordered on disdain. She inquired, with a pronounced emphasis on the word 'naturally,' whether these 'discerning and refined' residents were, in fact, aware of his presence and, more importantly, approved of his association with their daughter. One could hardly be too careful, she observed, in matters of social compatibility.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, feeling a desperate need to appear agreeable, hastened to assure Lady Bracknell that, of course, the residents of Belgrave Square were entirely aware of his… acquaintance with Miss Fairfax, and, he believed, viewed it with a most favorable eye. He trusted that their opinions were well known and, naturally, reflected a high degree of approval. He offered a slightly nervous smile, hoping to convey an air of confidence he did not entirely possess.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing’s nervous smile with a glacial indifference, and inquired, with a pointed lift of her eyebrow, whether these residents of Belgrave Square, in their supposed approval, had, perhaps, formally communicated their sentiments to her. One could hardly rely on mere hearsay, she observed, when the future happiness of one’s daughter was at stake.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, attempting to steer the conversation toward more familiar ground, hastened to explain that while he hadn't received a formal missive himself, he was quite certain that Miss Fairfax’s family, and indeed the esteemed residents of Belgrave Square, held him in the highest regard, a sentiment he was confident Lady Bracknell would soon discover firsthand. He added, with a touch of hopeful eagerness, that he was, in fact, planning a small gathering shortly to which he was delighted to extend an invitation to Lady Bracknell and her family.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing’s invitation with a degree of polite suspicion, and inquired whether this ‘small gathering’ was intended to be a formal affair, or merely a casual assemblage of individuals whose opinions, she suspected, might be… unreliable. One could scarcely allow a young lady’s future to be influenced by the whims of those lacking a demonstrable understanding of social decorum, she observed.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, feeling the pressure mounting, hastened to assure Lady Bracknell that the gathering would, of course, be conducted with the utmost formality and adherence to all established social protocols. He added that he would be delighted to furnish a complete list of the guests for her perusal, confident that she would find them to be individuals of impeccable standing and refined taste. A faint blush crept up his neck as he offered this reassurance, hoping desperately to placate her evident reservations.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing's offer of a guest list with a measured sigh, remarking that while a comprehensive roster was certainly appreciated, it would, of course, be necessary to ascertain the *precise* social standing of each individual listed. One could scarcely allow a future daughter-in-law to be associated with anyone of questionable lineage, she observed, her lips curving into a thin, almost imperceptible smile.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, eager to demonstrate his diligence, assured Lady Bracknell that he would, naturally, compile a detailed and meticulously researched dossier outlining the lineage and social accomplishments of each prospective guest, ensuring their suitability for her consideration. He added, with a slightly trembling voice, that he would be happy to present this document at her earliest convenience, hoping to alleviate any lingering concerns she might harbour. A bead of perspiration trickled down his temple.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing's offer of a detailed dossier with a look of profound skepticism, remarking that while such diligence was, theoretically, commendable, one could hardly rely solely on compiled documentation when assessing the true character of an individual; personal observation, she insisted, remained the ultimate arbiter of social worth. She paused, allowing her words to hang in the air, before adding that she would, of course, require a preliminary report, to be presented within the hour, detailing the lineage of at least three individuals, accompanied by a succinct assessment of their moral fibre.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, feeling increasingly flustered by the escalating demands, assured Lady Bracknell that he would, of course, undertake the task with the utmost diligence and dispatch, and would endeavor to provide the requested report within the stipulated hour. He added, with a slightly strained smile, that he was, naturally, quite familiar with the intricacies of genealogical research.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen, with a dramatic sigh, interrupted the increasingly fraught exchange, insisting that all this talk of lineage and dossiers was quite unnecessary. She declared to her mother that Mr. Worthing was, of course, perfectly suitable, and that any further investigation was simply a waste of precious time that could be spent planning the wedding. She looked expectantly at Jack, offering him a small, encouraging smile.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, attempting to regain some composure, assured Lady Bracknell that he possessed a remarkably extensive knowledge of several prominent families, and would, naturally, be delighted to furnish her with the preliminary report she requested; he hoped, he added with a nervous cough, that the hour would prove sufficient for such a comprehensive undertaking.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell regarded Mr. Worthing’s pronouncements with a barely perceptible arch of her eyebrow, and remarked that while a superficial familiarity with prominent families might be considered a modicum of preparedness, it hardly compensated for a demonstrable understanding of their *moral* standing. She added, with a pointed emphasis on the final word, that a wedding, after all, was a matter of the utmost gravity, and demanded far more than mere acquaintance with the social register.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack, attempting to appear confident despite the tremor in his voice, assured Lady Bracknell that he fully appreciated the gravity of the situation and the importance of moral standing. He added that he would certainly do his utmost to present a detailed and insightful assessment, hoping to demonstrate a thorough understanding of the families' virtues. He hoped, with a slightly anxious smile, that his efforts would prove satisfactory.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen informed Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell remarked that Gwendolen was not engaged to anyone and explained that an engagement should come as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, and that she or Gwendolen’s father would inform her of the fact. She added that it was hardly a matter for her to arrange for herself and then announced that she had a few questions to put to Mr. Worthing, instructing Gwendolen to wait for her below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen protested to Lady Bracknell.

opening.text: Lady Bracknell instructed Gwendolen to go to the carriage.

opening.text: Lady Bracknell repeated her instruction for Gwendolen to go to the carriage.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell invited Jack to take a seat.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack thanked Lady Bracknell but stated that he preferred standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell explained that she felt bound to tell Jack that he was not listed among the eligible young men, though she shared the same list as the Duchess of Bolton. She added that she was ready to enter his name if his answers were what a mother required and then inquired whether he smoked.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack admitted that he smoked.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell expressed her pleasure, stating that a man should always have an occupation and that there were too many idle men in London. She then asked him how old he was.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack replied that he was twenty-nine years old.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell commented that it was a very good age to be married and stated that she believed a man who desired to get married should know either everything or nothing, asking him which he knew.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack responded that he knew nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell expressed her pleasure, stating that she did not approve of anything that tampered with natural ignorance and that ignorance was like a delicate exotic fruit. She continued by criticizing modern education and suggesting that it would be dangerous to the upper classes. Finally, she asked about his income.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stated that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell inquired whether the income was in land or investments.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack clarified that it was chiefly in investments.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell observed that land had ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure and that it only provided position. She then asked about a country house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack explained that he had a country house with fifteen hundred acres attached, but that he did not depend on it for his income, adding that the poachers seemed to be the only ones benefiting from it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell inquired about the number of bedrooms in the country house and then asked if he had a town house.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack stated that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham, adding that he could get it back at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell expressed that she did not know Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack explained that Lady Bloxham did not go about very much and that she was considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell remarked that age was no guarantee of respectability of character and asked for the number of the house in Belgrave Square.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack replied that the number was 149.
